gaps: Geography is the largest gap. Across almost every domain, data are dense for Europe, North America and parts of Latin America and thin for Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and much of South and Southeast Asia: constituency-level election results before 2000, roll calls and bills, party-level data, court decisions, sub-national government and boundaries, parliamentary text and historical statistics all follow this pattern. Several of the few regional compilations that existed (the African Elections Database, the African Legislatures Project, regional elite datasets) are offline or were never publicly released.

Recent years are the second gap. Many canonical series stop between 2005 and 2021: MID, TIES and other Correlates of War files, Polity and most autocracy typologies, Archigos and REIGN, the Global Terrorism Database, the main protest datasets (SCAD, Mass Mobilization), religion-and-state data and several party expert surveys. For the most recent decade, researchers rely on a small number of continuously updated projects (V-Dem, UCDP, ACLED, Freedom House, the large survey programmes) and on event data, which changes what can be compared over time.

Some concepts have no maintained cross-national measure at all: executive decrees and unilateral powers outside the United States, legislative powers since the Parliamentary Powers Index, bureaucratic structure and political appointments, political prisoners and enforced disappearances, quota rules after 2015, green parties and environmental organisations, policy implementation and enforcement, informal lobbying and firms' political connections, the representation of Indigenous peoples, and a year-aware crosswalk for sub-national units, parties and politicians.

Access is becoming less stable. During the catalog's construction, about a dozen former project domains were found to serve unrelated or harmful content and were blocked; several U.S. federal tools were withdrawn and survive only in rescue archives; openICPSR was merged into ICPSR; OSF is ending new projects; and a growing share of producers (ACLED, GTD, OpenSecrets, ICPSR, several statistical offices) restrict automated or unregistered access. Many article-based datasets, especially historical ones, were never publicly released, which limits replication. Finally, citation counts could not be collected systematically because Google Scholar blocked automated checks, so adoption scores rest on documented uses and OpenAlex or Crossref counts recorded in the notes.
